name: Beth Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Beth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is kept confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior agent at the Coastline Homes branch in our seaside town, which is a franchise, so Gary owns our office and pays the brand a cut. We sell a lot of retirement flats on the seafront and holiday cottages, plus some lettings. I start with the AI assistant drafting replies to overnight enquiries, then it's viewings, mostly with retired couples moving down from the cities. I love it, I like the pace and I like that every day is different.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The legal side. Leaseholds on the retirement flats are a nightmare, with service charges and ground rent and all the rules, and I still get muddled. Nora, our senior negotiator, has to check my work on those. I'm good with the tools and the people, but I'm still learning the law bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but not a miracle, and that's fine by me. At work I'd keep showing Gary how it saves us time on enquiries. I'd post a bit about it, but I'm more interested in what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. I'd keep building my skills and maybe buy into the franchise one day. Josh and I own our terrace, which we renovated together, and I've got good savings, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Coastline and do a leasehold course to sort out my weak spot. I'd keep using AI for enquiries and listings every day. And I'd start saving towards buying a share of the franchise from Gary in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the terrace you renovated.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We bought a run-down two-up two-down when I was twenty-three, with help from my parents. Josh is a carpenter, so he did the kitchen and stairs, and I learned to plaster off videos. It's worth a good bit more now, which is most of our cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying into the franchise. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary's in his late fifties and he's said a few times he'd like someone to take over. I'd need maybe forty thousand, which is a lot, but with the house and savings it's not crazy. I'd rather own the business than be the junior forever.

say: I'd say AI is useful but **not a miracle**.
I'd keep showing the owner Gary how it **saves time** on enquiries.
think: I could build skills and **buy into the franchise** one day.
Our renovated **terrace** and savings mean I'm not worried.
do: **Take a leasehold course** to fix my weak spot.
Keep using AI daily for **enquiries and listings**.
**Save towards** buying a share of the franchise.
S0.quote: I'd rather own the business than be the junior forever.
fieldNote: She's openly **ambitious**, aiming to buy the franchise from Gary.
Her cushion is mostly the **renovated terrace** she and Josh did up.
She names **leasehold law** as her weak spot and plans a course.

steps.text: Take a leasehold law course this year
Use AI daily to answer overnight enquiries and draft listings
Save towards forty thousand to buy into the franchise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses to do more with fewer people, and that's how markets work. At work I'd volunteer to set up the new tools. At chapel I'd say people need to learn new skills, not wait for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I'm already the one using the tools, and if the admin and enquiries go to AI, Gary needs fewer staff but the ones he keeps are the quick ones. That could speed up the franchise plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd help Gary automate the enquiries, booking and follow-ups across the office. I'd ask him to give me more responsibility in return, like running lettings. And I'd keep saving for the franchise share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Gary needs fewer staff, who would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Liam, our admin, who books all the viewings. He's a nice lad but he hates computers. I'd want Gary to help him find another job locally, maybe in the council housing office, rather than just let him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should learn skills, not wait for help. What if they can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then family and church should step in first, and proper training after that. I just don't like the idea of people sitting at home on benefits. Work is good for people, even if it's different work.

say: I'd say small businesses can **do more** with fewer people.
I'd tell people at **chapel** to learn new skills, not wait.
think: I'm already using the tools, so I'm the **quick one** Gary would keep.
Fewer staff could **speed up** the franchise plan.
do: **Automate enquiries**, booking and follow-ups across the office.
S1.quote: Work is good for people, even if it's different work.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** first, consistent with her adaptability.
She wants Gary to help colleague Liam **find local work**, not just cut him.
Her **traditional views** shape her stance on benefits and family support.

steps.text: Automate enquiry replies, viewing bookings and follow-ups at Coastline Homes
Ask Gary to put her in charge of lettings
Keep adding to the franchise savings pot each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be tough, and families and communities will need to pull together. I'd say businesses should move fast and government should keep taxes low so people can start new things. At chapel I'd say we look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the franchise idea dies. If AI can do the thinking work by 2028, why would anyone pay a franchise fee for a brand and an office? The viewings might need a person until robots come in 2031, but there'd be far fewer agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the franchise plan and keep the savings safe. I'd look at hands-on property work, like buying run-down houses and doing them up with Josh, since he's a carpenter and we've done it once. I'd use AI to handle all the paperwork and marketing for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but I'd feel the ground going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doing up houses is a big risk if lots of people lose jobs. How would you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start small, one house at a time, and only buy cheap ones near the harbour. Josh would do the carpentry and I'd do the selling and plastering. If buyers dried up, we'd let them instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Josh that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancé Josh the agency job is probably gone, but our hands aren't. He's always said he wants to work for himself. This would be the push we needed.

say: I'd say families and communities must **pull together**.
I'd ask government to keep **taxes low** for new businesses.
think: The **franchise plan dies** if AGI arrives by **2028**.
Viewings last until **robots in 2031**, with far fewer agents.
do: **Drop the franchise** plan and keep savings safe.
**Do up run-down houses** with Josh, one at a time.
**Use AI** for all the paperwork and marketing.
S2.quote: I'd tell my fiancé Josh the agency job is probably gone, but our hands aren't.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** nature turns loss into a new business plan quickly.
She relies on Josh's **carpentry** and their past renovation.
She'd still **use AI** to run the thinking side of the new work.

steps.text: Drop the plan to buy into the Coastline Homes franchise
Buy one cheap house near the harbour to renovate with Josh
Use AI for the renovation paperwork, listings and marketing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ahead, and people who move early will be fine. At work I'd tell everyone to learn the tools now. At chapel I'd say the same, but more gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'd still lose the agent job eventually, but five years is enough to build a little renovation business on the side and have it ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Coastline and use the next two years to save and learn. Josh and I would buy our first renovation project in 2028 and do it up on weekends. By 2031 I'd want it to be our main income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to buy into the franchise in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. A franchise brand is only worth something if people need agents. I'd rather put that forty thousand into houses I can touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about family plans, would they change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably marry next year as planned, and think about children after the first renovation is done. My mum says I always plan everything, and she's right. I like knowing what's next.

say: I'd say people who **move early** will be fine.
I'd tell everyone at work to **learn the tools** now.
think: I'd still **lose the agent job** eventually.
Five years is enough to build a **renovation business** on the side.
do: **Keep working** at Coastline and save for two years.
**Buy a first renovation** project with Josh in 2028.
S3.quote: A franchise brand is only worth something if people need agents. I'd rather put that forty thousand into houses I can touch.
fieldNote: She'd shift money from the **franchise** into renovation property.
She plans **marriage and children** around the business timeline.
She expects to lose the agent job but feels **in control**.

steps.text: Keep working at Coastline Homes and save for two years
Buy a first renovation house with Josh in 2028
Marry Josh next year and plan children after the first renovation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so no excuses. At work I'd keep pushing the tools and planning. At chapel I'd say it's a time to prepare, not to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is great for me. I could buy into the franchise for a few years, make some money, then sell before AGI hits and move into renovation full-time. By 2036 I'd have a business and some houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a share of the franchise in about three years, run it lean with AI, and build up savings. Around 2032 I'd start the renovation business with Josh on the side. I'd sell my franchise share before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite excited. This is the one I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a franchise share and then selling it before AGI. Who would buy it from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair question. Maybe someone who doesn't see it coming, which I don't feel great about. Or I'd sell it back to the brand, if they'd have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you still do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but I'd be honest with any buyer about what I think is coming. I wouldn't want to sell someone a business I think is dying without telling them. My dad taught me that.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway**, so no excuses.
I'd tell chapel it's time to **prepare, not fear**.
think: I could **buy into the franchise** and sell before AGI.
By **2036** I'd have a business and some houses.
do: **Buy a franchise share** in about three years.
S4.quote: I wouldn't want to sell someone a business I think is dying without telling them. My dad taught me that.
fieldNote: She'd **buy and then sell** the franchise share before AGI.
Challenged on who'd buy it, she admits **discomfort** and commits to honesty.
Ten years makes her **ambitious**, not worried.

steps.text: Buy a share of the Coastline Homes franchise in three years
Start renovating houses with Josh around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the franchise plan would die before it started. What would help is low taxes and less red tape for people starting small businesses, and cheap loans for renovating empty houses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the retired couples who move here. Retired couples buying a seafront flat don't trust computers. Someone still needs to sit with them and explain the leasehold, or they'll get ripped off.

headlineQuote: Retired couples buying a seafront flat don't trust computers. Someone still needs to sit with them and explain the leasehold, or they'll get ripped off.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old junior agent** at a seaside franchise branch selling retirement flats and holiday cottages.
She uses **AI every day** and wants to buy into the franchise from its owner Gary.
She and her fiancé Josh, a carpenter, own a **renovated terrace** that forms most of their cushion.
Her **traditional views** show in trust in markets, family and chapel rather than benefits.
Under fast AGI she'd **renovate houses** with Josh; with more time she'd buy into the franchise first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the franchise plan would die before it started.
whatWouldHelp: **Low taxes**, less red tape, and **cheap loans** for renovating empty houses.
